span.label: Three of the best-described food webs in the ecological literature - Ythan estuary, Silwood Park and Little Rock Lake - treated as graphs and subjected to simulated species loss.
span.quote: our study is limited to the three richest and best-described food webs available in the ecological literature

span.label: How much of an ecosystem's fragility follows from the shape of its food web rather than from the ecology of the species in it?
span.quote: How dependent is ecosystem fragility from graph architecture?

span.label: Shows that food webs inherit the robust-yet-fragile signature of scale-free networks, and turns 'keystone species' from a qualitative label into a topological one that can be computed from the web.
span.quote: By using this method, it is the topology of the food web instead of the trophic position of species what determines which species are keystone.

span.label: mechanisms

span.quote: Our analysis shows that indeed, SF distributions are stable up to high values of f (more than 50% of species eliminated in the three food webs) when random removals occur, while those particular distributions quickly disappear under directed removal.

span.label: The approach lacks population dynamics and is constrained by the taxonomic resolution of the webs.
span.note: what this limits: every fragility estimate in the paper: THIS APPROXIMATION TO COMMUNITY FRAGILITY HAS OBVIOUS CAVEATS DERIVED FROM A LACK OF DYNAMICS AND TAXONOMIC LIMITATIONS
span.quote: This approximation to community fragility has obvious caveats derived from a lack of dynamics and taxonomic limitations.

span.label: The analysis treats food webs as undirected, unweighted graphs.

span.quote: Besides, our findings are based on a non-directed, and non-weighted graph.

span.quote: Because of the limitations of the available data in terms of both taxonomic resolution and size (Polis, 1991; Cohen et al., 1993; Williams and Martinez, 2000) our study is limited to the three richest and best-described food webs available in the ecological literature (figure 2).

span.note: RETRACTED: A JOIN KEY WITH A MEASURED ERROR RATE, RECORDED AS AN IDENTITY. The edge is `species --renamed-across-fields--> node`. The span: 'MOST nodes correspond to real species (88%) WHILE THE REST INVOLVE LOWER TAXONOMIC RESOLUTION.' Twelve per cent of the nodes are not species - they are genera, families, or aggregated trophic groups - and the authors say so in the same sentence they say the rest are. A `renamed-across-fields` edge says `node` is what this field calls a species, WHICH IS TRUE OF 88 PER CENT OF THEM. This is the sharpest form of the fault because the layer exists to be joined on: a reader joining ecological network nodes to a species list inherits a 12 per cent error and nothing in the edge tells them so. Compare the cell-type labels whose measured self-agreement is 70 per cent - SAME PROBLEM, DIFFERENT DISCIPLINE, AND NEITHER PAPER'S NUMBER SURVIVES INTO THE EDGE THAT USES ITS TERM. — strength of the relation: 1
